Obsolete

/AHB-suh-leet/ — stress on first syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is obsolete is no longer used because it has been replaced by something newer or better.

Fax machines are nearly obsolete, kept alive only by a few offices.

Worked Example

Eight-track tapes were made obsolete by cassettes, then CDs, then digital downloads—each technology rendering the previous one unnecessary and unusable.

Obsolete is vastly more precise than "old." A classic car is old but not obsolete; it still works and people choose to drive it. A fax machine is obsolete—it has been replaced by something better, and it's no longer useful for its original purpose. Obsolete means not just aged, but replaced and abandoned.

How Obsolete Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

outdated

outdated: behind the times though perhaps still usable

abandoned

abandoned: given up on and left behind entirely

archaic

archaic: so ancient it belongs to another era

Antonyms

current

current: in common use right now

cutting-edge

cutting-edge: the newest and most advanced available

How Strong Is It? — dated → old-fashioned → obsolete → defunct

dated vs. obsolete

dated vs. obsolete: Dated is much weaker than obsolete: something dated merely shows its age or feels out of style, while something obsolete has actually stopped being used at all.

old-fashioned vs. obsolete

old-fashioned vs. obsolete: Old-fashioned is stronger than dated but still weaker than obsolete — an old-fashioned tool belongs to an earlier era yet still works and gets used, while an obsolete one has been fully replaced.

defunct vs. obsolete

defunct vs. obsolete: Defunct is stronger than obsolete: an obsolete product has fallen out of use because something better replaced it, but a defunct one has ceased to exist or function entirely.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of obsolete.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — obsolescere

Root — obsolescere: to fall away from use (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Obsolete arrives as one solid piece of Latin: obsolescere, 'to fall away from use.' Inside Latin that word was built from ob- ('away') and solere ('to be in use'), but those parts fused long before English borrowed it - there is no prefix or suffix left to peel off. Something obsolete has done exactly what the Latin says: fallen away from use because something newer or better replaced it.

Use the root in a new word: obsolescence

Use the root in a new word: obsolescence: Engineers speak of planned obsolescence — designing products to wear out on purpose — a word that grows straight from the same Latin verb obsolescere, 'to fall out of use,' behind obsolete.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / technical

Obsolete is precise for technologies and products that have been replaced by something better. It's stronger than 'old' or 'outdated' because it implies the thing is no longer useful or functional. Use obsolete for technologies, products, or practices that have been superseded; use 'old-fashioned' for things merely out of style.
